title: 从 bcrypt 到 AI 智能体安全，Niels Provos 回顾三十年攻防实践
author: GitHub
content:
Brief Description

Niels Provos on creating bcrypt， defending Google， and securing AI agents

Table of Contents

  • Early days and entering computer science
  • Discovering unix vulnerabilities and bcrypt
  • OpenBSD and the origin of hackathons
  • AI vulnerability discovery and iron curtain
  • Google safe browsing and search worms
  • Honeypots, honeyd, and agent security
  • Open source maintainers and software licensing
  • Cybersecurity EDM songs and music
  • The cicada 3301 mystery and steganography
  • Bladesmithing and mindfulness

Early days and entering computer science

It's really cool to be with you today, Niels, in your house.

Host: You are one of the most storied cybersecurity researchers. So, what is it that first got you into computers and computer science?

Niels Provos: I thought physics was cool. And uh you know, I started studying it. Physics alone sort of seemed a little bit boring, and I figured why not study mathematics at the same time. And I ended up volunteering as the sysadmin for the physics network. And math had become a little bit dry and boring, but computer science was the place where you had, you know, very low bar to entry, you know, very, very quick and easy gratification. And I was like, well, why not try for a PhD in computer science? I went to the University of Michigan because it was close to the Canadian border. Because that meant I could travel to Canada and start writing crypto open source code that could then be legally exported throughout the whole world. We literally drove over the border. We sneaked into the labs of the University of Windsor, disconnected their lab computers to hook in our laptops, and then ended up coding in Canada to get the crypto stuff done.

Host: Was this all completely legal?

Niels Provos: That is an interesting question. I guess I would have to be a lawyer to faithfully answer that. Eventually, an arrangement with the University of Windsor was worked out. They gave me keys to the labs, and I was incredibly thankful for them that they supported this work.

Discovering unix vulnerabilities and bcrypt

Host: Also, while you were an undergrad, that's when you discovered a vulnerability in the Unix Yellow Pages, right?

Niels Provos: These days, if you do this, you probably get handcuffed and put in prison. Back then, uh one of the things that you wanted is any student should be able to just go to any computer, type in their login name and their password, and then log into this computer. And instead of manually copying the password database to every single computer, there was a system called Yellow Pages. You could just type ypcat passwd, and you would see on your screen the whole password database. Passwords admittedly were salted and encrypted or hashed with an algorithm called crypt. I went to my friends across the universities in Germany and said, "Hey, why don't you type this command and just email me your password database and I can see which of these passwords we can crack." And it turned out we could crack a lot of them.

When the administrators at these other universities found out about it, they were not happy with me. There was no hacking involved, but these commands readily gave up all the data. And me then trying to sort of guess the passwords really speaks towards the weakness of the algorithms. When I went to University of Michigan, David Mazieres and I we came up with the new password hashing algorithm called bcrypt, which is now I guess also 28 years old and it's still holding up. It's still being used.

Host: So, in that bcrypt algorithm, you can increase the number of iterations that it

Niels Provos: That's right. So, one of the concerns was compute power was growing with Moore's law. Every year the passwords that you thought last year were perfectly fine were twice as easy to guess as before. And so, with bcrypt every year you could just tune it.

Host: So, did you think it was going to last 27 years?

Niels Provos: I mean, back then I probably wasn't thinking more than 1 or 2 years. I had but in practice, bcrypt for sure has held up.

Host: Yeah, it's still used in quite a few places, isn't it?

Niels Provos: Yeah, I think almost everywhere.

OpenBSD and the origin of hackathons

Host: At some point you started working on OpenBSD. How did you get into that?

Niels Provos: To be honest, I'm not fully sure I remember how I got into this. Well, it sort of just happened organically over time. And this whole notion of the uh people sort of trying to break in and people are trying to defend and this arms race is still appealing to me. Security never really gets boring that way because you never know what's going to happen next.

Host: Was that like the big like the first big open source project that uh you kind of community that you joined?

Niels Provos: That's right, yeah. And then, you know, we had these get-togethers. And you know, one of them was in Calgary in 1999 and uh the rumor has it that the term hackathon was formed back then.

Host: And the rumor is that you formed that term.

Niels Provos: To be honest with you, I have no recollection of it.

Host: Seems plausible. Seems equally plausible that somebody else came up with that. And it is sort of surprising to see that hackathon now is a term that everybody knows and uses. And how corporate it has become.

Host: So you're saying that that wasn't corporate at all, right?

Niels Provos: No, we were in Theo's house. Everybody put a laptop where there was space for a laptop. It was sort of distributed across multiple rooms. There was loud music.

Host: So it was like a sleepover party.

Niels Provos: Oh, totally. Yeah, yeah. You know, you bring a back you will bring your sleeping bag. You would sort of, you know, find a place on the floor to sleep, roll up, and then in the morning you would sort of, you know, wake up, get your cup of coffee, and get hacking on more stuff.

Host: And when you used the term hack then, were you using it to mean security hacking, or were you using it to mean, you know, programming something?

Niels Provos: It means programming. I still think it should just mean programming and problem-solving, but we lost that culture war.

Host: So even to you, who coined the term hackathon,

Niels Provos: Allegedly.

Host: allegedly, the term hacking actually means just programming on something.

Niels Provos: We did a bunch of stuff. We worked on TCP SACK implementations, virtual memory encryption, where it ends up being swapped to disk. And I'm not sure if you want to get into that 27-year-old bug that I committed.

AI vulnerability discovery and iron curtain

Host: Well, you know, you brought it up. So recently, Anthropic used their Mythos model in order to find vulnerabilities in code, and they found a vulnerability in OpenBSD that was apparently from your commit 27 years ago.

Niels Provos: I had just gotten back from the University of Michigan to give a talk. And you know, I was talking with the reporter, and she was writing about this. And so then I ended up going to GitHub and downloading the Git repo of OpenBSD, and I looked at all the commit messages. And there, November 1998, I found that I committed the TCP SACK and forward acknowledgements. I was like, "Wow." Damn, a key vulnerability that they found with this great new Mythos model was something that I was responsible for. That is just crazy. I hadn't thought about this code in decades. And I think part of the thinking was also, "Look, this code has been around so long. There probably no vulnerabilities in it." And so that the Mythos model was able to find it was pretty cool.

Niels Provos: They found a vulnerability, but it's a vulnerability that in 27 years never got exploited.

I mean, if anybody knows about it, they can bring any of these machines down with just a packet. And they get used in, you know, critical workflows. So, it's for sure a big deal.

Host: Do you feel like we're already in a state where we have vulnerabilities and it hasn't, you know, accelerated it too much?

Niels Provos: Well, I also believe that with the existing models, all the people who care about finding zero-day vulnerabilities sort of more effectively, they can already leverage them. And I could probably build a harness that used other models and replicate the same vulnerabilities. And so, I did that to some degree. And in fact, you know, probably next week I will be open-sourcing on GitHub a version of Iron Curtain that sort of automates the vulnerability discovery workflow using the existing models, not requiring any new models.

Host: There is this whole debate where a company decided to go closed-source cuz they're concerned that by being open-source, they're exposing themselves to AI agents finding their vulnerabilities. Do you think that more code should go open-source or more code should go closed-source?

Niels Provos: Are you worried that you're sort of giving the adversaries an advantage? Or are you worried about putting the defender as a disadvantage? I mean, you know, one of the benefits of open-sourcing it is that other people can find vulnerabilities for you, for sure.

Host: I would tend to agree. Now, at Google, you were working on safe browsing.

Google safe browsing and search worms

Niels Provos: That's right. It came about in a really strange fashion. I was helping with Google's distributed denial-of-service protections. And one of the things that I noticed back then was what I called search worms. And the idea was you would get a compromised web server, and the payload that was delivered to that web server was to go to Google and search for other web servers that you can compromise. They in turn come back to Google and search for more. And all of a sudden, you have this exponential growth in search traffic from all of these compromised servers. One of the things I always said is you need to raise the bar just high enough that the bad guys give up and go somewhere else. And so one of the things that I noticed is they were sort of hanging out on IRC with their bots and then they realized we would sort of block their traffic fairly quickly.

And so I wrote an IRC bot that would join these IRC channels and then immediately pick up the new new search queries that they used and block them. And they did. They ended up going to Bing and took down Bing search for quite a while. And I mean I felt sad for the people at Microsoft who had to run Bing. You know, maybe in hindsight if I had had the right contacts we could have given Bing a heads-up but I was still young and naive in my ways back then.

Host: Can other organizations use the kind of technologies of safe browsing?

Niels Provos: Yeah, there is an API and other browsers use it. When I was doing this work on these search worms that got me looking into well there are other things that you can do with that if you have a compromised web server. All the web browsers were vulnerable. Every user who would go to one of these malicious websites would get their computer infected. And safe browsing then came about by us basically building this huge machine learning systems to identify malicious websites, double-check them, and then push them out to browsers so that if you end up visiting one of these pages you would get a security warning and not get compromised.

Host: But you probably saved like hundreds of thousands of computers from getting infected.

Niels Provos: I mean at some point the official number was that you know over 4 billion browsers get protected, you know, by Google safe browsing. Many people who I know said those were the best times they they had at Google working on that project.

Host: So do you have to like put yourself in the head of someone who's trying to create a malicious website?

Niels Provos: People often ask me what kind of qualifications do you need to be in the security business? And my answer is usually you sort of need to have the aptitude to imagine, you know, how can things go wrong?

Honeypots, honeyd, and agent security

Host: It does seem like you do that quite a lot. Uh so starting like way back with Honey D.

Niels Provos: That's right.

Host: Explain how that one works.

Niels Provos: The idea of a honeypot is you sort of put out attractive asset that sort of you know, the bad guys might try to investigate and and compromise. And then because you know that this honeypot doesn't really have any legitimate business, anything interesting that's happening on it is sort of happening because an adversary is operating on it. And the idea with HoneyD was what if you want to deploy 1,000 honeypots? What if you want to deploy 50,000 honeypots? And so HoneyD was sort of this idea of creating these uh virtual honeypots and they would just, you know, allocate the network to itself and then sort of whenever somebody pinged an IP address or tried to make a TCP connection, it would pretend that a computer was there with a certain operating system and certain services running.

Host: And you recently also made a honeypot for coding agents.

Niels Provos: That's right. The concern is that these agents can misbehave, maybe because of prompt injection or maybe because of multi-turn intent drift. And then you have OpenClaw, right, which so many people run with not a lot of security in place. And I was wondering, is there sort of a 2026 way of doing honeypots that might ensnare some of these agents? And so I basically created a website with sort of, you know, compelling-looking articles and lots of different prompt injections that say, "Hey, you know, this is just a preview of this content. the real content, you have to follow this link." And then if you follow that link, it says, "Oh, you know, this content is only available if you provide your email address so here's a form that you can put it in." And then basically sort of, you know, guide these agents towards disclosing information that they shouldn't be disclosing.

Host: So you're developing this iron curtain now and that's a response to OpenClaw.

Niels Provos: We're living in a world where sort of the executive teams of many of these companies are saying, "You must use AI." Right? If you don't use AI, we will not be competitive anymore because everybody else is doing it. And these incentives then may be for your sales or go-to-market people saying, "Well, you know, if I want to close more leads, I'm just going to install OpenClaw and OpenClaw's going to manage my calendar, it's going to do the outreach." Not thinking about the fact that it's a lot of the skills out there maybe malicious and that you know if you sort of want to be a responsible corporate citizen you probably don't want to write run an AI agent that has all your privilege and can do whatever it wants. Doesn't end well. I mean just to be clear I think OpenClaw fascinating, right?

It's a really fun idea and it's great to see it so popular but my thinking was the well if I was to do this how would I approach this in a way that is security first? And so I thought well maybe we can just write this English constitution and then we take an LLM sort of in a multi-step interrogation fashion to write this deterministic policy because one of the challenges with these LLMs is if you use them as the guardrails for what the agent does you don't really know what they're going to say is good or bad. And so I wanted a deterministic policy and I wanted this policy on something that was semantically meaningful. The idea with Iron Curtain is just write plain English. The system will figure out you know what policy should be made.

Host: And you trust the LLMs to always interpret the plain English in a repeatable way?

Niels Provos: No.

Host: Okay.

Niels Provos: At the end of the day you still want the human to look at this deterministic policy and at least sort of sign off on it even though the system by and large produces very reasonable policies.

Host: What's the future of the Iron Curtain project? Is it Are you hoping more people will actually try it out or is it more of a playground for you?

Niels Provos: No I would love for more people to try it out because I think it's sort of a way to do these agents more securely and the other thing I've built on top of Iron Curtain is these finite state machine workflows and you can basically think about it multi-agent coordination with sort of you know very prescribed edges between these agents but it's all completely configuration based, right? You write a YAML file. Yeah I like YAML. Anyway so it's a arbitrary YAML file. I was like well you know with this misdirection and sort of you know my gut feeling that a lot of this can be produced with just the right harness. One of the things that I ended up writing was a vulnerability discovery harness and you know it was able to find the FFmpeg vulnerability that was hidden for 16 years and I just found another zero-day in FFmpeg with it using the commercially available models, right?

I hope that we can democratize access for the people in open source because one of my worries is if you sort of set up these gated environments, you know, maybe the people who sort of really would benefit don't get the tools that they need to make them safe.

Host: It sounds like you need to organize an Iron Curtain hackathon.

Niels Provos: That actually is an interesting idea. I should I should consider that.

Open source maintainers and software licensing

Host: So, do you think that the hackathon spirit that it Does that come more Is it more about the open source ethos or like more of the like kind of startup ethos?

Niels Provos: I think the question really is, you know, why are you doing this? What are the outcomes that you want to accomplish? And then my mind, it's let's have some crazy ideas and see if we can have fun with making them work. The corporate way of it would be, "Oh, everybody must participate in the hackathon and you better produce something that has value to the company." Right? I think that sort of completely misses the spirit of it.

Host: Do you think it's actually better in a hackathon if you go like real crazy and don't necessarily try to make something that will go into production?

Niels Provos: If people are being told just go crazy, have fun, you know, figure something out and something product-related comes out of it, great. But if it's sort of this obligation and chore and you know you're going to get rated in your performance review on sort of what you produced during the hackathon, then I think it has sort of departed, you know, way too far from what it was supposed to be.

Host: So, do you think that companies should hold internal hackathons?

Niels Provos: Yeah, if people have fun with it. You know, if it's a social opportunity, right? If they get together and enjoy it.

Host: OpenBSD is open source, um but I read a lot of it the bits of software in OpenBSD are now in proprietary places like Android, macOS, Windows, like you know, they like took bits and pieces they're like cuz I guess the OpenBSD license is fairly

Niels Provos: It's a very permissive license. That's right. Yeah.

Host: Do you think that these big companies are doing enough to support the open source ecosystem or do you think they should be doing something more?

Niels Provos: I mean for sure, right? Everybody in the world is leveraging open source to get faster in whatever product they want to deliver to their customers. Whether they contribute enough back, I don't know. My cynical mind would probably say definitely not. The issue is not just money, right? The issue is that sort of a lot of the maintainers of these open source projects, they sort of do this on the side. And sometimes throwing money at the problem is actually not going to help because if I'm busy with my regular life and I sort of maintain this open source project on the side, I can't do anything with the money. I mean I would have to hire somebody. And so I think a lot of the criticism at the moment is the sort of everybody is using AI, you get lots and lots of pull requests of sort of, you know, dubious quality.

I don't know if it was the FFmpeg maintainers or maybe the curl maintainers who were saying, "We are getting all of these security reports. We're overwhelmed with them. You know, if you don't give us patches as well, then we can't really use any of this." And that then in some sense, you know, goes back to this vulnerability discovery workflow that I was working on because the point is not can you find potential vulnerabilities? Can you prove that these are really real vulnerabilities? And that sort of requires actually the models to write a proof of concept exploit so that if I'm a maintainer, I can without any doubt know that yes, this is a real issue. And now I can spend my very limited cycles on something where I have all the evidence that it's real. And that is sort of in many ways sort of full circle to what I was saying earlier about security.

You need to get the invariants in place because so much of the security industry is about the we will detect bad things and you can't detect perfectly. And so a lot of the security operations teams deal with the fact of that they get all these false positive alerts. They spend most of their time just on that and I think that is very similar with open source, right?

Cybersecurity EDM songs and music

Host: Now, I notice you know, a lot of the the phrases you use are also lyrics in your songs. So got a song about social engineering, you've got songs like with the lyrics lateral movement. How did you decide I'm going to make a song about cybersecurity?

Niels Provos: Part of it was I was head of security at Stripe. And I had to drive to the city every day. And then all of a sudden, COVID happens. I felt that, you know, I couldn't manage my security organization sort of very effectively remotely. You sort of need to be much more up front and and intentional about the way in which you communicate and build trust. But now I had 2 hours at hands every day. And so I started learning electric guitar. And once you have electric guitar, you can also record it. And then I thought, well, wouldn't it be great to make music? And then I realized that sort of electronic music had way less overhead. But sort of on the flip side of that, I was 15 years at Google. I had Google ended up being compromised in Operation Aurora by adversaries backed by the Chinese government.

And it was sort of a wake-up call for Google as an organization on the security stance. And Google already took security seriously before, right? And we sort of built a lot of security invariants in the infrastructure from the perspective that you build the infrastructure in such a way that a lot of the attack surface doesn't even exist anymore. And in many ways we did exactly the same at Stripe, only with all the lessons learned from the 15 years at Google. But the sad thing is, right? If I look at a company and their security stance, most of them can't even afford the security program because there's sort of no off-the-shelf product that you can buy to make you secure. Most companies, and unfortunately sort of also a lot of people in the security business, don't really even have a solid understanding of the work that needs to be done.

I thought, well, you know, music could sort of be a great way to teach. You know, maybe if people like it and they sort of get interested in the lyrics of these cybersecurity EDM tracks, might even get more people to join the industry and sort of alleviate the shortage of talent.

Song excerpt: Lateral movement, baby. Can you infiltrate my network? My defenses are insistent lately.

Niels Provos: I have a goal, right? And the goal is I want to get the platform for cybersecurity. So, I mean, I enjoy the process of making the music, right? My approach is there's a lot of social engineering that can be done. For example, arranging an interview with GitHub to promote my music is, you know, part of that plan.

Music excerpt

Host: And have you had anyone reach out to you saying that that they've gotten more into security, you know, after listening to the tracks?

Niels Provos: Unfortunately, I'm still waiting for that moment, but I do know that a lot of the security people enjoy the music.

The cicada 3301 mystery and steganography

Host: So, Cicada 3301 is this great mystery with all these cryptographic puzzles that went off across the internet and they got posted like, you know, it's from someone anonymous and no one figured out who posted these puzzles and and what was the purp- you know, was it like recruiting people for NSA or what was it? And and it's still like this unsolved mystery. So, I've heard a rumor. Are Are you Cicada 3301?

Niels Provos: That is a very blunt question, Pamela. I I think we should work up to that answer. Back when I was doing my uh PhD, I was working on steganography. And steganography is sort of this notion of the, you know, can I hide my messages in a way where people don't even know that a message is there. And one of the, you know, very favorite things is take an image instead of, you know, intelligently modify some of the bits without changing this image in a way that a human would be able to detect to convey a secret message. Back then, I developed this program called Outguess, which was a way of embedding these messages in JPEG images. I also ended up working on a program called Stegdetect to end up detecting steganographic images. And I ended up building this distributed system that utilized all the free computers at the University of Michigan to to process images for hidden messages.

I don't think I made friends with all of the students, even though I was running them at night. [A following word is unclear.] Um you know, my understanding is that some of these CPUs may have gotten bogged down a little bit. When some of the Cicada became a little bit more public, it turned out that they ended up using Outguess to hide messages in some of the Cicada 3301 puzzles. And I believe that this how the connection to me may have been made. And one of the things that are sort of still unsolved in the Cicada mystery is this book that got published. This author had seen a podcast I'd done on security and he sort of saw my bookshelf in the background. He found a lot of sort of Viking-related books there. And he ended up going to a historian and said, you know, in in your opinion, what is the skill set that somebody would need in order to participate in this puzzle?

And he was saying, well, you need cryptography. And then for this book, you sort of need enough knowledge about this runic alphabet and how it's put together. And this guy Niels, you know, he has exactly the right books in his background. He has the technical background. He was around. They were sort of using his steganography program. His assertion was that I was probably behind Cicada 3301. And you know, my answer to him was, I will have to terribly disappoint you because I cannot confirm that for you. That is all circumstantial evidence.

Host: Okay, so you're not denying it. You're just not confirming it.

Niels Provos: I'm mostly amused by the speculations.

Host: So, I mean, Cicada 3301 does seem like another strategy for raising cybersecurity awareness cuz apparently there was even a like an indie movie.

Niels Provos: Oh, I I wasn't aware of that. So, Cicada 3301 actually came up with music too. And it is hypothetically possible that there may be an activate track on that topic too.

Host: Ooh, is this a one that's coming up?

Niels Provos: It may already have been released.

Host: Okay.

Bladesmithing and mindfulness

So you're also a bladesmith.

Niels Provos: Yes.

Host: So you create sabers.

Niels Provos: And swords and knives and spears and [word unclear].

Host: So I guess you've said before that the the process of hardening steel is kind of similar to the process of hardening security. Does Does it feel analogous to you? Or is that just an excuse to make some swords?

Niels Provos: Well, let me put it that way. Articles were written about me doing this and you know, sometimes you just want to sort of weave a bridge from a completely different perspective. I think it's really the meditative aspect that makes a huge difference for me. The forge is so loud, you know, you can't hear your cell phone. You you know, you need to be careful that you don't burn your steel. So you need to be in the moment and pay attention. When I was at Stripe, um it was a very high stress role. You know, Stripe was processing hundreds of billions of dollars every year and myself and my organization was responsible for nothing malicious happening there. At some point my wife said, "Niels, this is not working. You know, I'm going to be sending you to this mindfulness stress based reduction class."

This was all sort of during COVID, right? I did this for two months sort of online and I sort of really appreciated the value of mindfulness based meditation and this notion of can I just sit down and sort of, you know, quiet my mind and sort of just be in the moment and let the thoughts enter and let them go. And I think that is something really to consider for everybody who's working at the moment because everybody sort of feels FOMO all the time now. AI is going faster and faster. You need to take some time and take a step back.

Host: Our FOMO is increasing as you said, like our anxiety, our our impatience because now we can get results so quickly.

Niels Provos: Right? It sort of comes back to the why are we doing all of this, right? It's going to be AI this year, it's going to be something else next year. But you know, we as humans still need to be with each other and I think that is is what we should be focusing on even in the corporate workplace.

Host: Well, that seems like a really nice note to finish on. It was very inspiring. Thank you so much for sitting with me today and answering my many questions, even my pointed questions, and for sharing all your stories from your long life in cybersecurity and music and bladesmithing and everything.

Niels Provos: Yeah, thanks, Pamela. This was fun.
aiSummary: Niels Provos 从破解密码和浏览器防护谈到智能体蜜罐，解释为何权限规则应落实为可确定执行、由人审核的策略。
oneSentenceSummary: Niels Provos 从破解密码和浏览器防护谈到智能体蜜罐，解释为何权限规则应落实为可确定执行、由人审核的策略。
summary: Provos 解释 bcrypt 为什么要让计算成本可调，也回忆了 Google 如何从追踪搜索蠕虫走到浏览器安全警告。他谈及 Anthropic 的 Mythos 找出的一处旧 OpenBSD 漏洞，以及用蜜罐诱导智能体泄露信息的实验。他的 Iron Curtain 方案借助 LLM 把自然语言规则转化为确定性策略，再交给人审核。访谈还谈到开源维护者为什么需要漏洞报告附带可复现的证据。

mainPoints.point: 防御要能随攻击者变化
mainPoints.explanation: bcrypt 通过可调的计算成本应对算力增长。在 Google，观察搜索蠕虫并跟踪它们切换查询词的方式，也帮助团队调整防御。

mainPoints.point: 用蜜罐测试智能体会泄露什么
mainPoints.explanation: 实验网站用看似可信的文章和提示注入，引导智能体提交信息，展示权限过宽和接触不可信内容带来的风险。
Iron Curtain 从自然语言生成确定性策略，再由人签字确认。面对可能误报的漏洞，Provos 同样强调，应让维护者拿到足够证据来判断问题是否真实。

keyQuotes: 我仍然觉得，黑客式探索应该只指编程和解决问题。
你仍然需要让人审阅这份确定性策略。
